subject: Banking
title: Too Big to Fail, Too Big to Jail
description: A micro-lesson that makes Too Big to Fail, Too Big to Jail usable.

hook.text: Since 2008, banks paid $321 billion in fines. Zero senior executives at major banks went to prison.

buildup.text: Prosecutors argued that jailing bank executives could destabilize the financial system.

discovery.text: Deferred prosecution agreements let banks avoid trial by paying fines and promising reform.

twist.text: Banks budget fines as operating costs. JPMorgan reserved $8.6 billion for legal fees in 2013 — and still profited.

climax.text: When fines are tax-deductible business expenses, enforcement becomes a tax, not a punishment.

punchline.text: $321 billion in fines. Zero top executives jailed.

quiz.question: How do banks treat regulatory fines?
options: As budgeted operating expenses and tax-deductible costs

details.summary: The phrase too big to jail describes how the largest banks avoid criminal prosecution because regulators fear that charges could collapse institutions deemed systemically important, creating a legal double standard.
details.whyItMatters: When banks are immune to criminal consequences, the deterrent effect of law evaporates. Executives can authorize misconduct knowing only the institution, not individuals, will face meaningful penalties.
takeaways: No major bank CEO has been criminally charged for crisis-era misconduct
Banks paid over $300 billion in post-crisis fines as institutions
Deferred prosecution agreements are the standard enforcement tool

faq.question: Why can't prosecutors charge big banks with crimes?
faq.answer: Prosecutors fear that criminal charges could cause a bank's counterparties and depositors to flee, triggering a systemic financial crisis. They use deferred prosecution agreements instead, which impose fines without the risks of trial.

faq.question: Is the too-big-to-jail problem being addressed?
faq.answer: The DOJ has announced policies to increase individual accountability, but results have been inconsistent. Until executives personally face criminal risk for institutional misconduct, the deterrent effect remains limited.
